title: UNIT 6: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
notes: ✓ Ecological interactions describe how organisms interact with one another and with their environment.

title: 6.1 TROPHIC LEVELS
notes:
✓ A trophic level is the position an organism occupies in a feeding sequence within an ecosystem.

1st trophic level → Producers
2nd trophic level → Primary consumers/herbivores
3rd trophic level → Secondary consumers/primary carnivores
Higher levels → Higher-level consumers

◆ Producers form the base because they introduce energy into the food system.
→ The position of an organism depends on how it obtains food.

title: 6.1.1 FOOD CHAIN
notes:
✓ A food chain is a sequence showing how food, energy and nutrients pass from one organism to another through feeding.

Example:
Grass → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake → Hawk

◆ Producer → makes food.
◆ Herbivore → feeds on producers.
◆ Carnivore → feeds on other animals.

→ Arrows show the direction of energy transfer: from the organism being eaten toward the organism that eats it.

title: FOOD WEB
notes:
✓ A food web is a network of interconnected food chains. It represents the complex feeding relationships within an ecosystem because most organisms eat or are eaten by more than one species.

→ Food webs are more realistic than single food chains because energy can move through several feeding pathways.

title: 6.1.2 FLOW OF ENERGY & MATTER THROUGH AN ECOSYSTEM
notes:
✓ Energy enters most ecosystems mainly from the Sun. Producers capture solar energy through photosynthesis and convert it into chemical energy stored in organic food.

Sun → Producers → Herbivores → Carnivores → Higher consumers

◆ Energy flows in one direction through trophic levels.
◆ Some energy is lost as heat during metabolic activities.
◆ Matter is different: nutrients are recycled between organisms and the physical environment.

✓ Energy flows; matter cycles.

title: ECOLOGICAL PYRAMIDS
notes:
✓ An ecological pyramid represents the structure of trophic levels in an ecosystem.

◆ Pyramid of energy → shows energy available at each trophic level; normally decreases toward higher levels.
◆ Pyramid of biomass → shows the amount of living biological material at each trophic level.
◆ Pyramid of numbers → shows the number of organisms at each trophic level.

→ Producers form the base, while higher consumers occupy upper levels.

title: 6.2.1 WATER CYCLE
notes:
✓ The water cycle is the continuous movement of water between the atmosphere, land, water bodies and living organisms.

◆ Evaporation → liquid water changes into water vapour.
◆ Transpiration → plants release water vapour.
◆ Condensation → water vapour cools and forms droplets/clouds.
◆ Precipitation → water falls as rain or other forms of precipitation.
◆ Runoff → water flows over land into rivers and other water bodies.
◆ Infiltration → water enters the soil and may become groundwater.

→ Solar energy drives much of the water cycle.

title: 6.2.2 CARBON CYCLE
notes:
✓ The carbon cycle describes the movement of carbon between the atmosphere, organisms, soil, water and geological materials.

◆ Photosynthesis → plants take in CO₂ and convert carbon into organic compounds.
◆ Feeding → carbon passes from producers to consumers.
◆ Respiration → organisms release CO₂.
◆ Decomposition → decomposers break down dead organisms and release carbon.
◆ Combustion → burning biomass and fossil fuels releases CO₂.
◆ Oceans → absorb and release carbon dioxide and store large amounts of carbon.

→ Carbon is essential for carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids.

title: 6.2.3 NITROGEN CYCLE
notes:
✓ Nitrogen is essential for amino acids, proteins and nucleic acids. Atmospheric nitrogen (N₂) cannot be directly used by most plants, so it must be converted into usable forms.

◆ Nitrogen fixation → atmospheric N₂ is converted into usable nitrogen compounds; nitrogen-fixing bacteria such as Rhizobium are important.

◆ Nitrification → ammonia/ammonium compounds are converted into nitrites and then nitrates by bacteria.

◆ Assimilation → plants absorb nitrogen compounds and incorporate nitrogen into organic molecules.

◆ Ammonification → decomposers convert organic nitrogen in dead matter and wastes into ammonia/ammonium compounds.

◆ Denitrification → bacteria convert nitrates back into atmospheric nitrogen.

title: RHIZOBIA & NITROGEN FIXATION
notes:
✓ Rhizobia are nitrogen-fixing bacteria associated with the root nodules of leguminous plants.

Legume roots ↔ Rhizobia

→ The bacteria convert atmospheric nitrogen into forms that can contribute to plant nutrition, while the plant provides the bacteria with suitable conditions and nutrients.

✓ This relationship improves soil nitrogen availability and supports plant growth.

title: BIOFERTILIZERS
notes:
✓ Biofertilizers contain living organisms that improve nutrient availability and soil fertility.

◆ Nitrogen-fixing microorganisms can increase available nitrogen.
◆ They can reduce dependence on chemical fertilizers.
◆ They are generally considered cost-effective and environmentally friendly.
◆ They can support crop productivity and sustainable agriculture.

→ Biofertilizers → useful microorganisms + improved nutrient availability.

title: 6.2.4 PHOSPHORUS CYCLE
notes:
✓ The phosphorus cycle describes the movement of phosphorus through rocks, soil, water and living organisms.

◆ Weathering → releases phosphate from rocks into soil and water.
◆ Plant uptake → plants absorb phosphate ions from soil.
◆ Feeding → animals obtain phosphorus by eating plants or other animals.
◆ Decomposition → phosphorus returns to soil and water from wastes and dead organisms.
◆ Sedimentation → phosphorus can accumulate in aquatic sediments and eventually form rocks.

→ Unlike carbon and nitrogen, phosphorus has no major atmospheric phase.

title: EUTROPHICATION
notes:
✓ Eutrophication is excessive growth of aquatic plants and algae caused by high nutrient inputs, especially nitrogen and phosphorus.

Fertilizer runoff → nutrient enrichment → algal bloom → decomposition → oxygen depletion → harm to aquatic organisms.

✓ Excess nutrients entering water bodies can reduce water quality and disturb aquatic ecosystems.

title: ATP & ENERGY TRANSFER
notes:
✓ ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the immediate energy source used for many cellular activities.

→ Energy released during cellular respiration is captured and stored in ATP, which can then provide energy for cellular processes.

title: UNIT 6 QUICK REVISION
notes:
◆ Trophic level → feeding position in an ecosystem.
◆ Producer → first trophic level.
◆ Primary consumer → herbivore.
◆ Secondary consumer → carnivore.
◆ Food chain → single feeding pathway.
◆ Food web → interconnected food chains.
◆ Energy → flows in one direction.
◆ Matter → cycles through ecosystems.
◆ Ecological pyramid → energy, biomass or numbers at trophic levels.
◆ Water cycle → evaporation → condensation → precipitation → runoff/infiltration.
◆ Carbon cycle → photosynthesis ↔ respiration + decomposition + combustion.
◆ Nitrogen cycle → fixation → nitrification → assimilation → ammonification → denitrification.
◆ Rhizobia → nitrogen-fixing bacteria associated with legume roots.
◆ Phosphorus cycle → mainly moves through rocks, soil, water and organisms.
◆ Eutrophication → excessive nutrient enrichment of water.
◆ ATP → immediate cellular energy source.
